title: Passive recon: OSINT
description: Discover assets without sending a single packet.

1.title: Subdomains
1.body:
## Certificate Transparency: the legal snitch

Since 2018, ALL TLS certificates must be recorded in the public
**Certificate Transparency (CT)** logs. This means that every subdomain someone
issued a certificate for is visible at:

```bash
# crt.sh — the most widely used search engine (replace victima.com)
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.victima.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_val' | sort -u
```

Tools that automate it: `sublist3r`, `assetfinder`, `amass` (the most complete).

## Other subdomain gold mines

- **Public DNS**: `dig any victima.com`; MX/NS/TXT records reveal providers.
- **Wayback Machine** (web.archive.org): old versions of the website with links to
  subdomains that no longer exist on the current site.
- **Google dorks**: `site:*.victima.com -www` (we'll see them below).
- **VirusTotal/Shodan**: aggregators that have already indexed those subdomains.

## The risk of the forgotten

`staging.victima.com` with an admin panel and default credentials, an
unauthenticated `jenkins.victima.com`, an exposed `.git/` on `dev.victima.com` —
all real, all found in seconds with CT logs. "Temporarily exposed"
environments last for years.

recon-pasivo-osint-t01-q01.prompt: What public database records ALL TLS certificates?
recon-pasivo-osint-t01-q01.hint: Certificate Transparency logs. The most widely used site to query them: crt.sh

recon-pasivo-osint-t01-q02.prompt: What DNS records reveal service locations?

recon-pasivo-osint-t01-q03.prompt: Why is dev.victima.com more dangerous than victima.com?
recon-pasivo-osint-t01-q03.hint: Development environments tend to have weaker security…

options.b: Development/staging environments often have default credentials, debug enabled and forgotten real data
options.d: Because it uses a different CDN

2.title: Google dorks and metadata
2.body:
## Google dorks: the search engine as a weapon

Google's advanced operators filter results with surgical precision:

```text
site:victima.com filetype:pdf          → all PDFs on the domain
site:victima.com inurl:admin           → pages with "admin" in the URL
site:*.victima.com -www                → indexed subdomains
filetype:env DB_PASSWORD               → exposed .env files (on any website!)
site:victima.com intitle:"index of"    → directory listings
```

The **GHDB** (at exploit-db.com/google-hacking-database) catalogs thousands of dorks by
category: credentials, error messages, vulnerable panels. Start there.

## Document metadata

PDF and Office documents carry embedded metadata: the author (the employee's name and email),
the file path on their PC (`C:\Users\jperez\Documentos\`), the software used, and sometimes
comments that were "visibly" deleted but can still be recovered.

Tools: `exiftool informe.pdf`, `metagoofil` (finds and extracts in bulk).

## Human OSINT (for the report)

LinkedIn reveals the structure of the IT team (who is the AD admin? Usernames
usually follow a pattern: `jperez`, `j.perez` — they get tested against the corporate
login in the active phase). The company's GitHub: code with forgotten
credentials (gitleaks automates this).

All of this without sending A SINGLE packet to the target: the sources are third parties
that have already indexed that information.

recon-pasivo-osint-t02-q01.prompt: What Google dork finds exposed config files?

recon-pasivo-osint-t02-q02.hint: Exploit-DB maintains it: dorks catalogued by category.

options.a: An alternative search engine to Google
options.b: A public database of catalogued dorks that find exposed files, credentials and panels

recon-pasivo-osint-t02-q03.prompt: What metadata leak is common in PDFs?

options.b: The private key of the website's TLS certificate
options.c: Usernames, emails and internal paths of the employees' computers

3.title: Passive to active
3.body:
## The invisible border

| Passive | Active |
|---|---|
| Queries to third parties (CT, Google, archive) | Packets TO the target |
| Undetectable | Detectable (logs, IDS, WAF) |
| Historical/aggregated information | Real current state |
| Always safe | Only with authorization |

You do NOT move to active until the scope is confirmed and you have written authorization
(the rules of engagement from module 1). Launching a scan against an out-of-scope host
is a legal incident.

## Transition checklist (your method)

After the passive phase, your target list should have:

1. **IPs/ranges** confirmed as belonging to the client (whois, DNS, CT logs).
2. **Subdomains** resolved to live IPs.
3. **Web surface**: URLs, panels, APIs detected.
4. **Potential users** (for credential attacks later on).

The next module (active recon) turns that list into: what is alive, what is running
and which version it has. The Nmap module automates it.

> **Take note**: every passive finding feeds the active phase. Every active finding
> feeds exploitation. It's a chain — and the pentester who skips links
> misses findings.

recon-pasivo-osint-t03-q01.prompt: What is the FUNDAMENTAL passive vs active difference?
recon-pasivo-osint-t03-q01.hint: Can the target detect what you are doing?

options.a: Passive uses free tools; active uses paid tools
options.b: Passive is manual; active is always automated
options.c: Active only applies to websites; passive to internal networks
options.d: In passive recon the target can't detect you; in active it can, because you send it packets

recon-pasivo-osint-t03-q02.prompt: You have collected: 15 subdomains, 3 employee emails and an exposed Jenkins panel. What is your next LOGICAL step in the active phase?
recon-pasivo-osint-t03-q02.hint: Verify what is alive and listening.

options.a: Launch an exploit against Jenkins immediately
options.b: Discover which hosts are alive and which ports/services they offer (host discovery + port scan)

4.title: Lab: OSINT against a real company
4.body:
## Practice: OSINT against TechCorp

The lab simulates the corporate website of "TechCorp Solutions". Everything you need is
PUBLICLY accessible — no exploits, just knowing where to look:

### 1. robots.txt
```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:18091/robots.txt
```

### 2. Source code (HTML comments)
```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18091/about | grep -i flag
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18091/ | grep -i admin
```

### 3. Configuration files
```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:18091/.env
```

### 4. Follow the clues
The HTML comments on the home page reveal that there is an admin panel. Follow the clue.

**This is exactly what an attacker does in the first 5 minutes against
any corporate website — without sending a single attack packet.**

recon-pasivo-osint-t04-q02.prompt: Find the flag in an HTML comment on /about.

recon-pasivo-osint-t04-q03.prompt: The .env file is accessible. Submit its flag.

recon-pasivo-osint-t04-q04.prompt: Follow the admin panel hint. Visit it and submit the flag.
recon-pasivo-osint-t04-q04.hint: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18091/ | grep admin → then curl /admin/panel

5.title: Lab: DNS enumeration
5.body:
## Zone Transfer: the DNS dump

The internal DNS of victima.com allows AXFR (zone transfer) to anyone:

```bash
# Normal query (record by record):
curl "http://127.0.0.1:18098/dig?name=www.victima.com"

# Zone transfer (ALL records at once):
curl "http://127.0.0.1:18098/axfr?server=ns1.victima.com"
```

The AXFR returns 14 records, including:
- `staging.victima.com` with a flag in the note field
- `internal.victima.com` with another flag
- `secret-admin.victima.com` — a hidden panel nobody should know about
- `_ldap._tcp` — reveals a Domain Controller

In a real pentest, an open AXFR is a critical finding: it exposes ALL of the
organization's internal infrastructure in a single request.

recon-pasivo-osint-t05-q01.prompt: Perform AXFR against ns1.victima.com. Submit the staging flag.

recon-pasivo-osint-t05-q02.prompt: How many records does the zone transfer return?
recon-pasivo-osint-t05-q02.hint: Count the entries in the AXFR JSON.
